claim: The WalRK two-component system was discovered over two decades ago and is among the most broadly conserved TCS in Firmicutes.
source: The WalRK two-component system (TCS) was discovered over two decades ago and is among the most broadly conserved TCS in Firmicutes (Fabret and Hoch, 1998; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Takada et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Fabret and Hoch, 1998; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Takada et al., 2018) that establish the discovery timeline and conservation of the WalRK system.

claim: WalK is a membrane-anchored sensor kinase.
source: WalK (also referred to as YycG, VicK, or MicA) is a membrane-anchored sensor kinase and WalR (also called YycF, VicR, or MicB) is a DNA binding response regulator of the OmpR family (Fabret and Hoch, 1998; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Dubrac and Msadek, 2008b; Okajima et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Fabret and Hoch, 1998; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Dubrac and Msadek, 2008b; Okajima et al., 2008) that characterize WalK as a membrane-anchored sensor kinase.

claim: WalR is a DNA binding response regulator of the OmpR family.
source: WalK (also referred to as YycG, VicK, or MicA) is a membrane-anchored sensor kinase and WalR (also called YycF, VicR, or MicB) is a DNA binding response regulator of the OmpR family (Fabret and Hoch, 1998; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Dubrac and Msadek, 2008b; Okajima et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Fabret and Hoch, 1998; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Dubrac and Msadek, 2008b; Okajima et al., 2008) that characterize WalR as a DNA binding response regulator of the OmpR family.

claim: In B. subtilis, WalH and WalI are negative regulators of the WalK sensor kinase.
source: In B. subtilis, WalH and WalI are negative regulators of the WalK sensor kinase and the three integral membrane proteins assemble into a multimeric complex (Szurmant et al., 2005; Szurmant et al., 2007; Szurmant et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Szurmant et al., 2005; Szurmant et al., 2007; Szurmant et al., 2008) that demonstrate the negative regulatory role of WalH and WalI on WalK.

claim: WalK, WalH, and WalI assemble into a multimeric complex.
source: In B. subtilis, WalH and WalI are negative regulators of the WalK sensor kinase and the three integral membrane proteins assemble into a multimeric complex (Szurmant et al., 2005; Szurmant et al., 2007; Szurmant et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Szurmant et al., 2005; Szurmant et al., 2007; Szurmant et al., 2008) that demonstrate the assembly of these three proteins into a complex.

claim: The WalRK system is essential in most Firmicutes.
source: The WalRK system is essential in most Firmicutes, making it an attractive antibiotic target (Barrett and Hoch, 1998; Gotoh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Barrett and Hoch, 1998; Gotoh et al., 2010) that establish the essentiality of the WalRK system in most Firmicutes.

claim: The WalR regulon contains genes encoding cell wall hydrolases in all cases where it has been examined.
source: In all cases where it has been examined, the WalR regulon contains genes encoding cell wall hydrolases (Bisicchia et al., 2007; Howell et al., 2003; Ahn and Burne, 2007; Ng et al., 2005; Liu, 2006; Dubrac et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to six studies (Bisicchia et al., 2007; Howell et al., 2003; Ahn and Burne, 2007; Ng et al., 2005; Liu, 2006; Dubrac et al., 2007) that demonstrate the presence of cell wall hydrolase genes in the WalR regulon.

claim: Cells engineered to constitutively express a subset of WalR-regulated enzymes can bypass the essentiality of the WalRK signaling pathway.
source: Furthermore, cells engineered to constitutively express a subset of these enzymes can bypass the essentiality of the signaling pathway (Ng et al., 2003; Delaune et al., 2011; Takada et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Ng et al., 2003; Delaune et al., 2011; Takada et al., 2018) that demonstrate bypass of WalRK essentiality through constitutive expression of target enzymes.

claim: CwlO and LytE are critical for cell wall elongation in B. subtilis.
source: Cells lacking either PG hydrolase are viable but depletion of one in the absence of the other causes a cessation of growth followed by lysis (Bisicchia et al., 2007; Hashimoto et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Bisicchia et al., 2007; Hashimoto et al., 2012) that demonstrate the critical role of CwlO and LytE in cell wall elongation through synthetic lethality experiments.

claim: Both CwlO and LytE are D,L-endopeptidases that cleave the peptide bond between the second (γ-D-Glu) and third (mDAP) amino acid in the stem peptide of PG.
source: Both enzymes are D,L-endopeptidases and cleave the peptide bond between the second (γ-D-Glu) and third (mDAP) amino acid in the stem peptide of PG (Ishikawa et al., 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Ishikawa et al., 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 2004) that characterize the enzymatic activity and cleavage specificity of these enzymes.

claim: CwlO is controlled by a membrane complex composed of the non-canonical ABC transporter FtsEX and two integral membrane proteins SweC and SweD.
source: CwlO is controlled by a membrane complex composed of the non-canonical ABC transporter FtsEX and two integral membrane proteins SweC and SweD (Meisner et al., 2013; Domínguez-Cuevas et al., 2012; Brunet et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Meisner et al., 2013; Domínguez-Cuevas et al., 2012; Brunet et al., 2019) that demonstrate the regulatory control of CwlO by the FtsEX-SweC-SweD complex.

claim: LytE is a secreted enzyme with LysM domains that direct it to the lateral cell wall.
source: LytE is a secreted enzyme with LysM domains that direct it to the lateral cell wall (Margot et al., 1998; Ishikawa et al., 1998; Buist et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Margot et al., 1998; Ishikawa et al., 1998; Buist et al., 2008) that characterize LytE as a secreted enzyme with LysM domains that target it to the lateral cell wall.

claim: LytE levels increase approximately 2-fold in the absence of CwlO.
source: In the course of characterizing LytE protein levels in various mutant backgrounds, we discovered that LytE levels increase approximately 2-fold in the absence of CwlO (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating increased LytE protein levels in the ΔcwlO mutant compared to wild-type.

claim: Transcription from the PlytE promoter increased ~2 fold in the ∆cwlO mutant.
source: As can be seen in Figure 1B, transcription from the PlytE promoter increased ~2 fold in the ∆cwlO mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating increased PlytE-lacZ expression in the ΔcwlO mutant.

claim: A similar increase in PlytE transcription was observed in cells lacking the FtsEX complex.
source: A similar increase in PlytE transcription was observed in cells lacking the FtsEX complex, which is required for CwlO activity (Figure 1B) (Meisner et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating increased PlytE-lacZ expression in the ΔftsEX mutant, and by citation to Meisner et al., 2013 establishing that FtsEX is required for CwlO activity.

claim: A point mutation in the Walker A motif in FtsE predicted to impair ATP binding resulted in increased lytE transcription.
source: Furthermore, a point mutation in the Walker A motif in FtsE, predicted to impair ATP binding (Yang et al., 2011; Meisner et al., 2013) but not CwlO association with FtsX (Brunet et al., 2019) also resulted in increased lytE transcription (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrating increased PlytE-lacZ expression in the ftsE(D162A) mutant, and by citations to studies (Yang et al., 2011; Meisner et al., 2013; Brunet et al., 2019) characterizing the mutation.

claim: Cells lacking CwlO activity increase expression of lytE.
source: From these experiments we conclude that cells lacking CwlO activity increase expression of lytE.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing increased lytE transcription in ΔcwlO, ΔftsEX, and ftsE(D162A) mutants.

claim: A modest but reproducible increase in lytE transcription was observed in cells lacking LytE.
source: We also observed a modest but reproducible increase in lytE transcription in cells lacking LytE (Figure 1B), suggesting that B. subtilis increases lytE expression in response to reduction in D,L-endopeptidase activity in general.
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating increased PlytE-lacZ expression in the ΔlytE mutant.

claim: B. subtilis increases lytE expression in response to reduction in D,L-endopeptidase activity in general.
source: We also observed a modest but reproducible increase in lytE transcription in cells lacking LytE (Figure 1B), suggesting that B. subtilis increases lytE expression in response to reduction in D,L-endopeptidase activity in general.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that lytE transcription increases not only when CwlO is absent but also when LytE itself is absent, suggesting a general response to reduced D,L-endopeptidase activity.

claim: Cells lacking cwlO were shorter and fatter than wild-type.
source: As reported previously, cells lacking cwlO were shorter and fatter than wild-type and these morphological phenotypes were largely homogenous throughout the population (Hashimoto et al., 2012; Meisner et al., 2013; Brunet et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three previous studies (Hashimoto et al., 2012; Meisner et al., 2013; Brunet et al., 2019) that reported this morphological phenotype.

claim: The ΔcwlO mutant cells had intact membranes based on cytoplasmic mCherry fluorescence and propidium iodide staining.
source: Furthermore, based on cytoplasmic mCherry fluorescence (Figure 1C) and propidium iodide staining (Figure 1D), the ∆cwlO mutant cells had intact membranes.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and 1D demonstrating retention of cytoplasmic mCherry and low propidium iodide staining in ΔcwlO cells.

claim: Cells lacking cwlO in which LytE was artificially maintained at wild-type levels had heterogeneous morphologies with >20% lysis or membrane permeability defects.
source: By contrast, cells lacking cwlO in which LytE was artificially maintained at wild-type levels had heterogeneous morphologies with >20% lysis or membrane permeability defects (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1C, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrating heterogeneous morphologies and increased lysis/membrane permeability in ΔcwlO cells with LytE maintained at wild-type levels.

claim: The increase in LytE levels allows the ∆cwlO mutant to maintain membrane integrity and a homogenous morphology.
source: These results indicate that the increase in LytE levels allows the ∆cwlO mutant to maintain membrane integrity and a homogenous morphology.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the comparison of ΔcwlO cells with elevated LytE (intact membranes, homogenous morphology) versus ΔcwlO cells with LytE at wild-type levels (membrane defects, heterogeneous morphology).

claim: Cells lacking CwlO compensate for the reduction in D,L-endopeptidase activity by increasing expression of a second D,L-endopeptidase, LytE.
source: Thus, these data suggest that cells lacking CwlO compensate for the reduction in D,L-endopeptidase activity by increasing expression of a second D,L-endopeptidase, LytE.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that ΔcwlO cells increase LytE expression and that this increase is necessary for maintaining cell envelope integrity.

claim: Cells with increased levels of wild-type LytE had reduced lytE transcription.
source: Strikingly, cells with increased levels of wild-type LytE had reduced lytE transcription, while cells over-expressing the catalytic mutant had PlytE promoter activity similar to wild-type (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 2A and immunoblot data in Figure 2B demonstrating reduced PlytE-lacZ expression when wild-type LytE is overexpressed.

claim: Cells over-expressing the LytE catalytic mutant (C247S) had PlytE promoter activity similar to wild-type.
source: Strikingly, cells with increased levels of wild-type LytE had reduced lytE transcription, while cells over-expressing the catalytic mutant had PlytE promoter activity similar to wild-type (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 2A and immunoblot data in Figure 2B demonstrating that PlytE-lacZ expression remains similar to wild-type when the catalytic mutant LytE(C247S) is overexpressed.

claim: All cells lacking cwlO had increased Venus fluorescence from the PlytE-venus reporter.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2C, all cells lacking cwlO had increased Venus fluorescence while all cells over-expressing lytE had reduced fluorescence.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating increased PlytE-venus fluorescence in all ΔcwlO cells.

claim: All cells over-expressing lytE had reduced Venus fluorescence from the PlytE-venus reporter.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2C, all cells lacking cwlO had increased Venus fluorescence while all cells over-expressing lytE had reduced fluorescence.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating reduced PlytE-venus fluorescence in all cells overexpressing lytE.

claim: B. subtilis modulates lytE expression in response to both an increase and decrease in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that B. subtilis modulates lytE expression in response to both an increase and decrease in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing increased lytE expression when D,L-endopeptidase activity is low (ΔcwlO) and decreased lytE expression when D,L-endopeptidase activity is high (lytE overexpression).

claim: PlytE transcription inversely correlated with the amount of D,L-endopeptidase produced.
source: As can been seen in Figure 2D, we found that PlytE transcription inversely correlated with the amount of D,L-endopeptidase produced.
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 2D and immunoblot data in Figure 2E demonstrating an inverse correlation between LytE levels and PlytE-lacZ expression across a range of IPTG concentrations.

claim: At IPTG concentrations used to express lytE, all cells in the population had equivalent GFP fluorescence from the Phyperspank-gfp construct.
source: Importantly, using the same IPTG-regulated promoter fused to gfp, we found that at IPTG concentrations similar to those used to express lytE all cells in the population had equivalent GFP fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 demonstrating uniform GFP expression across the cell population at various IPTG concentrations.

claim: The graded response to changes in LytE levels observed in ensemble assays reflects similar changes in D,L-endopeptidase levels in all cells in the population.
source: Thus, the graded response to the changes in LytE levels observed in the ensemble assays reflect similar changes in D,L-endopeptidase levels in all cells in the population.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that the IPTG-inducible promoter produces uniform expression across the population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the graded response in ensemble assays reflects population-wide changes rather than heterogeneity.

claim: The lytE gene has two promoters that influence each other.
source: The lytE gene is has two promoters that influence each other (Tseng et al., 2011; Salzberg et al., 2013) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Tseng et al., 2011; Salzberg et al., 2013) that characterized the dual promoter structure of lytE, and by the schematic shown in Figure 3A.

claim: One lytE promoter is recognized by the alternative sigma factor Sigma I (SigI).
source: One is recognized by the alternative sigma factor Sigma I (SigI) and the other is controlled by Sigma A (SigA) but requires the phosphorylated form of the response regulator WalR (Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Salzberg et al., 2013 that characterized the two promoters of lytE.

claim: The other lytE promoter is controlled by Sigma A (SigA) but requires the phosphorylated form of the response regulator WalR.
source: One is recognized by the alternative sigma factor Sigma I (SigI) and the other is controlled by Sigma A (SigA) but requires the phosphorylated form of the response regulator WalR (Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Salzberg et al., 2013 that characterized the two promoters of lytE.

claim: Cells lacking SigI have reduced PlytE-lacZ expression and reduced LytE protein levels.
source: Cells lacking SigI have reduced PlytE-lacZ expression and reduced LytE protein levels, while cells lacking the anti-SigI factor RsgI have increased lytE transcription and increased LytE protein levels (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 3B and immunoblot data in Figure 3C demonstrating reduced PlytE-lacZ expression and LytE protein levels in ΔsigI cells.

claim: Cells lacking the anti-SigI factor RsgI have increased lytE transcription and increased LytE protein levels.
source: Cells lacking SigI have reduced PlytE-lacZ expression and reduced LytE protein levels, while cells lacking the anti-SigI factor RsgI have increased lytE transcription and increased LytE protein levels (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 3B and immunoblot data in Figure 3C demonstrating increased PlytE-lacZ expression and LytE protein levels in ΔrsgI cells.

claim: A point mutation in one of the two WalR binding sites in the lytE promoter (box2*) abolishes lytE transcription and LytE protein levels.
source: Similarly, a point mutation in one of the two WalR binding sites in the lytE promoter (box2*) (Salzberg et al., 2013) abolishes lytE transcription and LytE protein levels (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 3B and immunoblot data in Figure 3C demonstrating abolished PlytE-lacZ expression and LytE protein levels in the box2* mutant, and by citation to Salzberg et al., 2013 that characterized the WalR binding sites.

claim: Cells lacking WalH have increased lytE transcription and LytE protein levels.
source: Furthermore, cells lacking WalH, a negative regulator of the WalRK two-component system (Szurmant et al., 2005), results in increased lytE transcription and LytE protein levels (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 3B and immunoblot data in Figure 3C demonstrating increased PlytE-lacZ expression and LytE protein levels in ΔwalH cells, and by citation to Szurmant et al., 2005 that characterized WalH as a negative regulator.

claim: Cells lacking SigI or harboring a point mutation in the WalR binding site in the lytE promoter are inviable when CwlO is depleted.
source: Consistent with these observations and the synthetic lethal relationship between lytE and cwlO, cells lacking SigI or harboring a point mutation in the WalR binding site in the lytE promoter are inviable when CwlO is depleted (Salzberg et al., 2013) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 3D demonstrating inviability of ΔsigI and box2* mutants when CwlO is depleted, and by citation to Salzberg et al., 2013.

claim: Over-expression of lytE in the ∆rsgI mutant resulted in reduced lytE transcription.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3E, over-expression of lytE in the ∆rsgI mutant resulted in reduced lytE transcription, while in the ∆walH mutant lytE transcription was unchanged.
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 3E demonstrating reduced PlytE-lacZ expression when lytE is overexpressed in the ΔrsgI mutant.

claim: In the ∆walH mutant, lytE transcription was unchanged when lytE was over-expressed.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3E, over-expression of lytE in the ∆rsgI mutant resulted in reduced lytE transcription, while in the ∆walH mutant lytE transcription was unchanged.
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 3E demonstrating unchanged PlytE-lacZ expression when lytE is overexpressed in the ΔwalH mutant.

claim: The WalRK signaling pathway is responsible for mediating the observed response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: These data suggest that the WalRK signaling pathway is responsible for mediating the observed response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that the response to lytE overexpression is maintained in the ΔrsgI mutant but abolished in the ΔwalH mutant, suggesting WalRK mediates the response.

claim: yocH is positively regulated by phosphorylated WalR (WalR ~P).
source: yocH is positively regulated by phosphorylated WalR (WalR ~P) while iseA is negatively regulated by WalR ~P (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the schematic diagram in Figure 4A showing WalR~P activating yocH transcription.

claim: iseA is negatively regulated by WalR ~P.
source: yocH is positively regulated by phosphorylated WalR (WalR ~P) while iseA is negatively regulated by WalR ~P (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the schematic diagram in Figure 4A showing WalR~P repressing iseA transcription.

claim: In the absence of WalH or WalI, WalR activity is high and PyocH-venus transcription increased.
source: In the absence of either, WalR activity is high and PyocH-venus transcription increased, while PiseA-venus transcription decreased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B demonstrating increased PyocH-venus fluorescence in ΔwalH and ΔwalI cells.

claim: In the absence of WalH or WalI, PiseA-venus transcription decreased.
source: In the absence of either, WalR activity is high and PyocH-venus transcription increased, while PiseA-venus transcription decreased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A demonstrating decreased PiseA-venus fluorescence in ΔwalH and ΔwalI cells.

claim: Depletion of WalRK resulted in strong de-repression of PiseA-venus.
source: Furthermore, and as expected, depletion of WalRK resulted in strong de-repression of PiseA-venus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C demonstrating strong de-repression of PiseA-venus upon WalRK depletion.

claim: PyocH transcription increased in the absence of CwlO.
source: When monitored by ß-galactosidase assay, PyocH transcription increased in the absence of CwlO and decreased when lytE, but not lytE(C247S), was over-expressed (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating increased PyocH-lacZ expression in ΔcwlO cells.

claim: PyocH transcription decreased when lytE was over-expressed.
source: When monitored by ß-galactosidase assay, PyocH transcription increased in the absence of CwlO and decreased when lytE, but not lytE(C247S), was over-expressed (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 4C demonstrating decreased PyocH-lacZ expression when lytE is overexpressed.

claim: PyocH transcription did not decrease when lytE(C247S) was over-expressed.
source: When monitored by ß-galactosidase assay, PyocH transcription increased in the absence of CwlO and decreased when lytE, but not lytE(C247S), was over-expressed (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 4C demonstrating that PyocH-lacZ expression does not decrease when the catalytic mutant lytE(C247S) is overexpressed.

claim: PiseA transcription was reduced in the absence of CwlO.
source: Reciprocally, PiseA transcription was reduced in the absence of CwlO and was strongly de-repressed when lytE was over-expressed (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating reduced PiseA-lacZ expression in ΔcwlO cells.

claim: PiseA transcription was strongly de-repressed when lytE was over-expressed.
source: Reciprocally, PiseA transcription was reduced in the absence of CwlO and was strongly de-repressed when lytE was over-expressed (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 4C demonstrating strong de-repression of PiseA-lacZ expression when lytE is overexpressed.

claim: Within 30 min after shutting off cwlO transcription, PyocH-directed transcription of venus increased.
source: Within 30 min after shutting off cwlO transcription, PyocH-directed transcription of venus increased (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4D demonstrating increased PyocH-venus fluorescence 30 min after CwlO depletion.

claim: 15 min after inducing lytE transcription, de-repression of the PiseA-venus reporter was detected.
source: Furthermore, 15 min after inducing lytE transcription, we could detect de-repression of the PiseA-venus reporter (Figure 4E and G), and after 30 min down-regulation of the PyocH-venus was apparent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and 4G demonstrating de-repression of PiseA-venus 15 min after lytE induction.

claim: After 30 min of lytE induction, down-regulation of the PyocH-venus was apparent.
source: Furthermore, 15 min after inducing lytE transcription, we could detect de-repression of the PiseA-venus reporter (Figure 4E and G), and after 30 min down-regulation of the PyocH-venus was apparent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 demonstrating down-regulation of PyocH-venus 30 min after lytE induction.

claim: The WalR-specific promoters PyocH and PiseA were not affected by a deletion of sigI.
source: Importantly, these WalR-specific promoters were not affected by a deletion of sigI (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B), nor were their dynamics altered in the ∆sigI mutant in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 4B and 4C, and fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and 3B demonstrating that PyocH and PiseA expression is not affected by ΔsigI.

claim: The dynamics of PyocH and PiseA were not altered in the ∆sigI mutant in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: Importantly, these WalR-specific promoters were not affected by a deletion of sigI (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B), nor were their dynamics altered in the ∆sigI mutant in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C demonstrating that the response of PiseA-venus to lytE overexpression is similar in wild-type and ΔsigI cells.

claim: Cells lacking lytE have a modest but reproducible increase in CwlO.
source: Furthermore, cells lacking lytE have a modest but reproducible increase in CwlO (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B demonstrating increased CwlO protein levels in ΔlytE cells.

claim: Cells over-expressing lytE have low levels of CwlO.
source: Immunoblots to monitor the levels of CwlO in cells over-expressing lytE indicate that this is indeed the case (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A demonstrating low CwlO protein levels when lytE is overexpressed.

claim: The WalRK signaling pathway monitors the extent of D,L endopeptidase activity and modulates lytE and cwlO transcription in response.
source: Taken together with the data in Figure 3E, these results suggest that the WalRK signaling pathway monitors the extent of D,L endopeptidase activity and modulates lytE and cwlO transcription in response.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that WalR-regulated promoters (PyocH, PiseA) and WalR-dependent genes (lytE, cwlO) respond to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.

claim: The serine/threonine kinase PrkC also controls WalR activity.
source: Recent studies indicate that the serine/threonine kinase PrkC also controls WalR activity (Libby et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Libby et al., 2015 that demonstrated PrkC control of WalR activity.

claim: PrkC principally regulates WalR in stationary phase.
source: PrkC principally regulates WalR in stationary phase and therefore was unlikely to mediate the response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity during exponential growth observed here.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PrkC function from the cited study (Libby et al., 2015).

claim: The transcriptional responses of PiseA and PyocH to lytE overexpression were similar in the presence and absence of PrkC.
source: As anticipated, the transcriptional responses were similar in the presence and absence of PrkC, ruling out a role for this signaling kinase in responding to D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 demonstrating similar responses of PiseA-venus and PyocH-venus to lytE overexpression in wild-type and ΔprkC cells.

claim: PrkC does not have a role in responding to D,L-endopeptidase activity during exponential growth.
source: As anticipated, the transcriptional responses were similar in the presence and absence of PrkC, ruling out a role for this signaling kinase in responding to D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that the response to D,L-endopeptidase activity is unchanged in the ΔprkC mutant.

claim: WalK localizes to the divisome in an FtsZ-dependent manner.
source: Previous work on the WalRK pathway indicates that WalK, but not WalH or WalI, localizes to the divisome and does so in an FtsZ-dependent manner (Fukushima et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fukushima et al., 2008 that demonstrated WalK localization to the divisome.

claim: Depletion of FtsZ or other divisome components resulted in a decrease in yocH mRNA levels and an increase in pdaC transcript levels.
source: Furthermore, depletion of FtsZ or other divisome components resulted in a decrease in yocH mRNA levels and an increase in pdaC transcript levels, consistent with a reduction in WalR activity (Fukushima et al., 2008; Fukushima et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Fukushima et al., 2008; Fukushima et al., 2011) that demonstrated changes in WalR-regulated gene expression upon divisome depletion.

claim: lytE over-expression resulted in similar de-repression of PiseA-venus in wild-type and cells lacking a divisome.
source: As can be seen in Figure 5A, lytE over-expression resulted in similar de-repression of PiseA-venus in wild-type and cells lacking a divisome.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A demonstrating similar de-repression of PiseA-venus upon lytE overexpression in both wild-type and mciZ-expressing (division-inhibited) cells.

claim: Depletion of CwlO in filamenting cells for 30 min triggered induction of PyocH-venus to the same extent as CwlO depletion in wild-type cells.
source: Reciprocally, depletion of CwlO in filamenting cells for 30 min triggered induction of PyocH-venus to the same extent as CwlO depletion in wild-type cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating similar induction of PyocH-venus upon CwlO depletion in both wild-type and mciZ-expressing (division-inhibited) cells.

claim: The WalRK signaling pathway is capable of responding to changes in PG hydrolase activity in the absence of division.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that the WalRK signaling pathway is capable of responding to changes in PG hydrolase activity in the absence of division, and therefore argue that WalK can function along the lateral membranes.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that WalR-regulated reporters respond to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity in cells where division is blocked by MciZ expression.

claim: WalK can function along the lateral membranes.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that the WalRK signaling pathway is capable of responding to changes in PG hydrolase activity in the absence of division, and therefore argue that WalK can function along the lateral membranes.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that WalRK signaling responds to changes in lateral wall hydrolases (CwlO and LytE) even when division is blocked.

claim: Basal WalRK activity was unaffected by deletions of the ECDs of WalH and WalI.
source: Previous work from Szurmant and Hoch showed that basal WalRK activity was unaffected by deletions of the ECDs of WalH and WalI (Szurmant et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Szurmant et al., 2008 that demonstrated basal WalRK activity is maintained when the extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are deleted.

claim: Expression of both the full-length and truncated alleles of walH and walI restored basal PiseA-venus transcription.
source: Similar to what was reported previously, expression of both the full-length and truncated alleles of walH and walI restored basal PiseA-venus transcription (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 demonstrating that both full-length and ΔECD variants of WalH and WalI restore basal PiseA-venus expression.

claim: Cells harboring the full-length and truncated alleles of walH and walI responded similarly to wild-type when lytE was over-expressed.
source: Importantly, cells harboring the full-length and truncated alleles of walH and walI responded similarly to wild-type when lytE was over-expressed (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 demonstrating that cells with full-length or ΔECD variants of WalH and WalI show similar de-repression of PiseA-venus upon lytE overexpression.

claim: The extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are not individually required for WalRK signaling in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: These data indicate that the extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are not individually required for WalRK signaling in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that deletion of the extracellular domain of either WalH or WalI individually does not prevent the response to lytE overexpression.

claim: Cells lacking the extracellular domains of both WalH and WalI can respond to lytE over-expression, although the response was more modest.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6B, in both strains PiseA-venus transcription was de-repressed upon over-expression of lytE, although the response was more modest in the strain harboring the deletion variants.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B demonstrating de-repression of PiseA-venus upon lytE overexpression in cells expressing both WalH(ΔECD) and WalI(ΔECD), though the response is reduced compared to full-length proteins.

claim: The extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are not necessary for WalRK signaling in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: Collectively, these data argue that the extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are not necessary for WalRK signaling in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity and suggest that the extracellular domain of WalK functions as the sensor.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that cells lacking the extracellular domains of both WalH and WalI can still respond to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.

claim: The extracellular domain of WalK functions as the sensor for D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: Collectively, these data argue that the extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are not necessary for WalRK signaling in response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity and suggest that the extracellular domain of WalK functions as the sensor.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that the extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are not required for the response, suggesting WalK's extracellular domain is the sensor.

claim: WalK contains a 148 amino acid extracellular loop that is homologous to Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS)-like domains, also known as an sCache domain.
source: WalK contains a 148 amino acid extracellular loop that is homologous to Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS)-like domains, also known as an sCache domain (Upadhyay et al., 2016) (Figure 6A – schematic).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Upadhyay et al., 2016 that characterized the sCache domain in WalK, and by the schematic shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PAS-like domains are a common feature of sensor kinases and in some cases have been shown to bind signaling ligands.
source: These domains are a common feature of sensor kinases and in some cases have been shown to bind signaling ligands (Chang et al., 2010; Henry and Crosson, 2011; Upadhyay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Chang et al., 2010; Henry and Crosson, 2011; Upadhyay et al., 2016) that demonstrate PAS-like domains are common in sensor kinases and can bind ligands.

claim: Deletion of the extracellular sCache domain of WalK (WalK∆sCache) results in constitutive signaling and high WalR activity.
source: Previous studies indicate that deletion of the extracellular sCache domain of WalK (WalK∆sCache) results in constitutive signaling and high WalR activity (Fukushima et al., 2011) and we confirmed this using both PyocH-venus and PiseA-venus reporters (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fukushima et al., 2011 and by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating high PyocH-venus and low PiseA-venus expression in WalK∆sCache cells.

claim: The ∆walK mutant harboring the walK(∆sCache) variant was unresponsive to lytE over-expression.
source: However, the ∆walK mutant harboring the walK(∆sCache) variant was unresponsive to lytE over-expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7B demonstrating that PiseA-venus is not de-repressed upon lytE overexpression in cells expressing WalK∆sCache.

claim: The walK(∆sCache) variant failed to respond to depletion of CwlO.
source: Furthermore, the walK(∆sCache) variant failed to respond to depletion of CwlO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 demonstrating that PyocH-venus is not induced upon CwlO depletion in cells expressing WalK∆sCache.

claim: The sCache domain of WalK is necessary for sensing changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that the sCache domain of WalK is necessary for sensing changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that deletion of the sCache domain abolishes the response to changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.

claim: A strong interaction was observed when T25-WalK and T18-WalH were co-expressed with untagged WalI in the BACTH assay.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6C, a strong interaction was only observed when T25-WalK and T18-WalH were co-expressed with untagged WalI, indicating that all three proteins are required for stable interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by BACTH assay data shown in Figure 7C demonstrating a strong interaction (blue colonies) when T25-WalK, T18-WalH, and untagged WalI are co-expressed.

claim: All three proteins (WalK, WalH, and WalI) are required for stable interaction in the BACTH assay.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6C, a strong interaction was only observed when T25-WalK and T18-WalH were co-expressed with untagged WalI, indicating that all three proteins are required for stable interaction.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the BACTH assay data showing that interaction is only observed when all three proteins are present.

claim: A similarly strong interaction was observed using T25-WalK(∆sCache) in the BACTH assay.
source: Importantly, we observed a similarly strong interaction using T25-WalK(∆sCache) (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by BACTH assay data shown in Figure 7C demonstrating a strong interaction (blue colonies) when T25-WalK(ΔsCache), T18-WalH, and untagged WalI are co-expressed.

claim: The WalK variant lacking its ECD stably interacts with WalH and WalI in vivo.
source: These data argue that the WalK variant lacking its ECD stably interacts with WalH and WalI in vivo.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the BACTH assay data showing that WalK(ΔsCache) interacts with WalH and WalI.

claim: The extracellular sCache domain of WalK functions as the sensing domain that monitors changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: Collectively, these results and those from Figure 5 suggest that the extracellular sCache domain of WalK functions as the sensing domain that monitors changes in D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observations that (1) the sCache domain is required for the response to D,L-endopeptidase activity, (2) the extracellular domains of WalH and WalI are not required, and (3) WalK(ΔsCache) still interacts with WalH and WalI.

claim: The chimeras containing D,L-endopeptidase domains from LytF and CwlS de-repressed PiseA transcription.
source: Consistent with the idea that WalK monitors D,L-endopeptidase activity, the chimeras that contained D,L-endopeptidase domains from PG hydrolases that function in cell separation (LytF and CwlS from B. subtilis) (Ohnishi et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 2003; Fukushima et al., 2006) de-repressed PiseA transcription (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B demonstrating de-repression of PiseA-venus when M3-LytF or M3-CwlS chimeras are overexpressed, and by citations characterizing these enzymes (Ohnishi et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 2003; Fukushima et al., 2006).

claim: WalK signaling was not impacted by expression of chimeras containing D,D-endopeptidase, L,D-endopeptidase, amidase, or glucosaminidase domains.
source: By contrast, WalK signaling was not impacted by expression of chimeras containing D,D-endopeptidase domains (MepM and MepS from E. coli) (Singh et al., 2012), L,D-endopeptidase domains (LytH and CwlK from B. subtilis) (Horsburgh et al., 2003; Fukushima et al., 2007), the amidase domain from B. subtilis YrvJ (Wendrich and Marahiel, 1997), or the glucosaminidase domain from B. subtilis LytD (Margot et al., 1994) (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B demonstrating no de-repression of PiseA-venus when chimeras with other hydrolase domains are overexpressed, and by citations characterizing these enzymes.

claim: The MepM D,D-endopeptidase chimera was able to suppress the lethality of ∆cwlO ∆lytE double mutant but did not impact PiseA transcription.
source: Over-expression of most of the chimeras did not cause discernable morphological defects raising the possibility that the fusions were not active enough to alter WalRK signaling, however, we note that the MepM D,D-endopeptidase chimera was able to suppress the lethality of ∆cwlO ∆lytE double mutant (Hashimoto et al., 2018) but even this fusion did not impact PiseA transcription (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A demonstrating that the M3-MepM chimera can suppress ΔcwlO ΔlytE lethality, and by citation to Hashimoto et al., 2018, but fluorescence data shows no impact on PiseA-venus.

claim: WalK specifically monitors D,L-endopeptidase activity.
source: Collectively, these data favor the model that WalK specifically monitors D,L-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that only D,L-endopeptidase chimeras, but not other types of PG hydrolases, trigger a WalRK response.

claim: Only the cleavage products generated by D,L-endopeptidase digestion reduced WalRK activity and de-repressed PiseA-venus.
source: Notably, only the cleavage products generated by D,L-endopeptidase digestion reduced WalRK activity and de-repressed PiseA-venus (Figure 8E - bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8E (bottom panels) demonstrating that only soluble products from D,L-endopeptidase (CwlOΔcc) digestion of sacculi de-repress PiseA-venus, while products from amidase or muramidase digestion do not.

claim: The soluble material from sacculi incubated with iodoacetamide-inactivated CwlO∆cc failed to reduce WalRK activity.
source: Furthermore, the soluble material from sacculi incubated with iodoacetamide-inactivated CwlO∆cc failed to reduce WalRK activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 demonstrating that soluble products from sacculi incubated with inactivated CwlOΔcc do not de-repress PiseA-venus.

claim: WalK specifically responds to D,L-endopeptidase cleavage products.
source: These results indicate that WalK specifically responds to D,L-endopeptidase cleavage products.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that only D,L-endopeptidase cleavage products, and not products from other PG hydrolases or inactivated enzyme, trigger a WalRK response.

claim: When D,L-endopeptidase activity is low, the concentration of cleavage products drops leading to an increase in WalK kinase activity and a concomitant increase in WalR ~P.
source: When D,L-endopeptidase activity is low, the concentration of these cleavage products drops leading to an increase in WalK kinase activity and a concomitant increase in WalR ~P.
evidence: The claim is a model/inference based on the experimental data showing that low D,L-endopeptidase activity (ΔcwlO) leads to increased WalR-dependent transcription.

claim: WalR ~P increases transcription of lytE and cwlO, restoring homeostasis.
source: WalR ~P increases transcription of lytE and cwlO, restoring homeostasis (Figure 9 – left panel).
evidence: The claim is a model/inference based on the experimental data showing that WalR~P activates lytE and cwlO transcription, and that this compensates for low D,L-endopeptidase activity.

claim: When there is elevated D,L-endopeptidase activity, the concentration of cleavage products increases.
source: Reciprocally, when there is elevated D,L-endopeptidase activity, the concentration of cleavage products increases.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference based on the relationship between enzyme activity and product generation.

claim: High concentrations of D,L-endopeptidase cleavage products reduce WalK activity, resulting in a decrease in lytE and cwlO transcription.
source: High concentrations of these putative allosteric inhibitors reduce WalK activity, resulting in a decrease in lytE and cwlO transcription (Figure 9 – right panel).
evidence: The claim is a model/inference based on the experimental data showing that high D,L-endopeptidase activity (lytE overexpression) leads to decreased WalR-dependent transcription.

claim: The iseA gene encodes a secreted inhibitor of D,L-endopeptidases.
source: The iseA gene, which is repressed by WalR ~P, encodes a secreted inhibitor of D,L-endopeptidases (Bisicchia et al., 2007; Salzberg and Helmann, 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Bisicchia et al., 2007; Salzberg and Helmann, 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2008) that characterized IseA as a secreted inhibitor of D,L-endopeptidases.

claim: LytE is likely to be the primary target of IseA.
source: However, we have found that LytE is likely to be the primary target of IseA.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing that IseA overexpression affects cell elongation (LytE-dependent) but not cell separation.

claim: The levels of IseA needed to inhibit LytE had no impact on cell separation.
source: Specifically, we found that the levels of IseA needed to inhibit LytE had no impact on cell separation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and 1B demonstrating that IseA overexpression affects cell elongation but not cell separation.

claim: CwlO has a half-life of ~7 min.
source: Furthermore, we have also found that CwlO has a half-life of ~7 min (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2A demonstrating rapid turnover of CwlO protein after translation inhibition.

claim: When D,L-endopeptidase activity is too high, a drop in WalRK signaling causes a reduction in lytE and cwlO transcription, inhibition of LytE activity via de-repression of iseA, and a reduction in CwlO levels through degradation or shedding.
source: Accordingly, when D,L-endopeptidase activity is too high, a drop in WalRK signaling not only causes a reduction in lytE and cwlO transcription, but also inhibition of LytE activity via de-repression of iseA and a reduction in CwlO levels through degradation or shedding of the enzyme into the medium (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is a model/inference based on experimental data showing transcriptional changes, IseA de-repression, and CwlO turnover in response to high D,L-endopeptidase activity.

claim: The WalRK signaling pathway is able to adjust the levels and activity of CwlO and LytE on the time-scale of a cell cycle to maintain homeostatic control of these essential enzymes during growth.
source: Thus, the WalRK signaling pathway is able to adjust the levels and activity of CwlO and LytE on the time-scale of a cell cycle to maintain homeostatic control of these essential enzymes during growth.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the kinetic data showing rapid responses (15-30 min) of WalR-regulated genes and the short half-life of CwlO.

claim: The WalRK pathway functions in the homeostatic control of cell wall hydrolases by sensing the cleavage products generated by these enzymes.
source: Here, we report that the WalR-WalK (WalRK) two-component signaling pathway functions in the homeostatic control of the cell wall hydrolases required for expansion of the PG during growth.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The WalRK two-component system functions in the homeostatic control of the cell wall elongation hydrolases LytE and CwlO by sensing and responding to PG cleavage products generated by these enzymes.
source: Altogether, our data support a model in which the WalR-WalK two-component signaling pathway functions in homeostatic control of the cell wall elongation hydrolases LytE and CwlO, and does so by sensing and responding to PG cleavage products generated by these enzymes (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in the model shown in Figure 9.

claim: This represents the first homeostatic pathway for cell wall hydrolysis in bacteria.
source: This represents the first homeostatic pathway for cell wall hydrolysis in bacteria and we propose that cell wall remodeling in related Gram-positive pathogens is subject to similar regulatory control.
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the findings and the lack of previously reported homeostatic control mechanisms for cell wall hydrolysis.

claim: Cell wall remodeling in related Gram-positive pathogens is subject to similar regulatory control.
source: This represents the first homeostatic pathway for cell wall hydrolysis in bacteria and we propose that cell wall remodeling in related Gram-positive pathogens is subject to similar regulatory control.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the conservation of the WalRK system in Gram-positive pathogens and the similarity of their WalR regulons.

claim: The WalRK pathway is conserved among many Gram-positive pathogens where it controls transcription of distinct sets of PG hydrolases.
source: The WalR-WalK pathway is conserved among many Gram-positive pathogens where it controls transcription of distinct sets of PG hydrolases.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature about the conservation and function of WalRK in pathogens.

claim: The WalRK two-component system can be found in important human pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Listeria monocytogenes, Bacillus anthracis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Streptococcus mutans.
source: The WalRK two-component system is the most broadly conserved TCS in the Firmicutes and can be found in important human pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Listeria monocytogenes, Bacillus anthracis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Streptococcus mutans (Dubrac et al., 2008a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dubrac et al., 2008a that documented the conservation of WalRK across Firmicutes pathogens.

claim: In most cases, the WalRK pathway is essential in Gram-positive pathogens.
source: In most cases, this pathway is essential and, in the organisms in which it has been investigated, the WalR regulon contains cell wall hydrolases although not necessarily D,L-endopeptidases (Martin et al., 1999; Howell et al., 2003; Dubrac and Msadek, 2004; Ng et al., 2005; Liu, 2006; Bisicchia et al., 2007; Ahn and Burne, 2007; Delaune et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting the essentiality of WalRK in various pathogens.

claim: The essentiality of the WalRK pathway can be bypassed by engineering bacteria to express a subset of the PG hydrolytic enzymes in the WalR regulon.
source: Furthermore, as is the case with B. subtilis (Takada et al., 2018), the essentiality of this pathway can be bypassed by engineering these bacteria to express a subset of the PG hydrolytic enzymes in the WalR regulon (Ng et al., 2003; Delaune et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Ng et al., 2003; Delaune et al., 2011; Takada et al., 2018) demonstrating bypass of WalRK essentiality through constitutive expression of target enzymes in various bacteria.

claim: The WalRK pathway functions in homeostatic control of cell wall hydrolysis in Gram-positive pathogens and uses distinct cleavage products to monitor PG hydrolase activity.
source: Based on these similarities, we hypothesize that the WalRK pathway functions in homeostatic control of cell wall hydrolysis in these pathogens and uses distinct cleavage products to monitor PG hydrolase activity.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis/speculation based on the conservation of WalRK and the findings in B. subtilis.

claim: The WalK sensor kinases in Streptococci and Lactococci lack an extracellular sCache domain.
source: It is noteworthy that the WalK sensor kinases in Streptococci and Lactococci lack an extracellular sCache domain (Lange et al., 1999; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Lange et al., 1999; Dubrac et al., 2008a; Wang et al., 2013) that characterized WalK in these organisms.

claim: If there is homeostatic control of cell wall hydrolases in Streptococci and Lactococci, they must use a different sensing mechanism or employ a distinct signaling pathway.
source: Accordingly, if there is homeostatic control of cell wall hydrolases in these bacteria they must use a different sensing mechanism or employ a distinct signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference based on the absence of the sCache domain in WalK from these organisms.

claim: The StkP serine/threonine kinase in S. pneumoniae has been implicated in modulating cell wall hydrolysis and has been suggested to function in concert with WalRK pathway.
source: Intriguingly, the StkP serine/theronine kinase in S. pneumoniae has been implicated in modulating cell wall hydrolysis and has been suggested to function in concert with WalRK pathway in this organism (Fleurie et al., 2012; Stamsås et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Fleurie et al., 2012; Stamsås et al., 2017) that implicated StkP in cell wall hydrolysis regulation in S. pneumoniae.
